newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Re-election win already priced into Brazil markets.
newsitem.headline: Re-election win already priced into Brazil markets.

text.p: Passage of Brazil's re-election bill is already priced into local stocks so an initial nod by lawmakers would more likely prompt a spate of profit-taking than a buying spree Wednesday, analysts said.
"The market has anticipated its approval," said Sergio Goldman, an analyst with BBA Paribas. "The market tends to buy on the rumor and sell on the fact."
The Chamber of Deputies began meeting this afternoon for an initial vote on a constitutional amendment that would allow President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to run again in 1998.
Analysts said that, after an initial gleeful uptick, local shares are likely to dip if the bill is approved as investors rake in gains from a roughly 10 percent run-up this year.
Stock prices and volumes have risen sharply due to investor optimism that Congress will pass the re-election bill, which will allow the government to move on to pressing economic reforms.
As a result, an initial lower house nod on re-election will not spark a stampede by investors looking to snap up Brazilian shares, but rather a mild sell-off.
"My impression is there could be a small correction," said Quentin Lewis, an equities analyst at Bozano, Simonsen.
"I don't see it as some sort of stimulus that will cause investment managers to change their weightings or pension funds to start chucking money into Brazil," he added.

But some market watchers said bolsa reaction Wednesday would depend on the government's margin of victory. The market expects the amendment to pass with up to 340 votes compared with 308 needed for the required two-thirds majority.
"The reaction will be more a function of the margin of victory than approval itself," BBA's Goldman said.
"If it passes by 360 or more, the market will rise strongly because the government will be in a stronger position. But if it passes by a slim margin, the market will fall," he added.
Even passage by a slight margin, however, would please investors, who would gradually pump more money into Brazilian equities over the medium term as the approval process advances, analysts said.
If passed tonight, the amendment still faces a second lower house vote followed by two votes in the Senate.
Defeat in the lower house tonight would prompt a sharp drop in Brazilian bolsas as investors shed positions to re-assess the country's political scenario, analysts said.
The market favors re-election because it would provide the framework for political continuity and boost Cardoso's economic reform program, which has been bogged down in the Brazilian Congress
"Re-election would mean a lengthening of the investment horizon," Lewis said.
